title: Split-Brain Laboratory
summary: Two staged experiments about the logic of a lateralised trial. In the first, learners build a trial - item, visual field, response channel, corpus callosum - commit to a prediction and run it, until they have found a combination the section changes and one it does not. In the second, the trial that classically fails is fixed and the five conditions it depends on can be switched off one at a time, turning a famous finding into an ordinary one. Nothing is presented to a visual field; the tool reports what a deliberately simplified routing model gives.
learningObjectives: Work out, for any combination of visual field and response channel, whether a disconnected hemisphere can answer.
Explain why the split-brain findings are a statement about routing rather than about what each hemisphere is for.
Name at least three methodological conditions that would make the classic demonstration stop working.
Distinguish a result that challenges an account from a result produced by a procedural failure.
State why split-brain evidence does not support left-brained or right-brained descriptions of people.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab. Nothing is presented to the reader's visual field and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native select, radio, checkbox and button controls throughout, each with an accessible name. The routing diagram is hidden from assistive technology and carries a visible sentence inside its own figure naming the item, the receiving hemisphere, the channel asked with, the state of the callosum and the outcome - the diagram is pinned while the tables scroll away, so the pin reads on its own. Nothing in the drawing is carried by colour: the active route is a thick solid line against thin dashed ones, active boxes carry a heavier border and their own label text, and the section is drawn as a cross over a gap as well as being named. Each experiment has its own pinned primary and the inactive one is hidden, so only one is ever visible; measured heights at 1366 by 768 are 419px for experiment 1 and 229px for experiment 2. The condition explanations of experiment 2 sit outside the pinned block so that the pin cannot grow past its budget. A live goal checklist writes '(met)' or '(not yet)' into the text rather than relying on the marker. Every trial, preset and condition change announces through the shell's polite live region, and focus moves to the laboratory heading when the prediction unlocks it. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers, heading levels do not skip, forced colours are handled, and there is no horizontal page scroll at 320px, 375px, 1366px, 1440px or 1920px.
readmeTopic: Why the split-brain findings are about routing rather than about what each hemisphere is for, and what the classic demonstration quietly depends on
simulationNotes: A deliberately simplified routing model, stated as such on the page. Each visual field projects to the opposite hemisphere; each hand is controlled by the opposite hemisphere; speech is produced by the left hemisphere; with the callosum intact whatever one hemisphere receives is available to the other; after a complete section a response succeeds only when the hemisphere that received the item also controls the channel asked with. That gives twelve combinations: all twelve succeed with the callosum intact, and after a section the three that succeed are right field with speech, right field with the right hand, and left field with the left hand. Experiment 2 fixes the trial at left field, spoken report, complete section and lists five conditions it depends on - brief presentation, monitored fixation, a complete section including the splenium, controlled cross-cueing, and left-only speech in this individual. Losing fixation monitoring makes the trial uninterpretable; breaking any of the other four lets the word be reported without disturbing the routing account. Deliberate simplifications: nothing is presented to a visual field because a browser cannot control fixation or duration, real performance varies with material, task, interval, practice and individual, speech is not left-lateralised in everyone, and many disconnected right hemispheres read simple words. The four items are ordinary words invented for this page; no published stimulus, image or procedure is reproduced and no real participant appears.
